hints: Think about what type of mechanism this is, free radical substitution starts in a very specific way.
Compare the bond strengths, the Cl-Cl bond is much weaker than the C-H bond and is broken first to start the chain.
Remember light causes equal splitting of electrons to make highly reactive species with unpaired electrons, not charged ions.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the reaction type**

This is free radical substitution of an alkane. It needs highly reactive chlorine radicals to start the chain reaction.

Overall initiation idea:
$$\text{CH}_4 + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

**See what light does in initiation**

Light provides exactly the right energy for homolytic fission of the weak Cl-Cl bond. Each Cl atom keeps one electron from the shared pair.

Initiation step:
$$\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$$

**Link to the rest of the mechanism**

Once formed, the $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$ radicals attack $\text{CH}_4$ in propagation. Light is not needed to break C-H directly or to heat the mixture, its job is just to create the initial radicals.

options.A: C-H bonds are strong (about 410 kJ mol-1) and are not broken by light directly. They are broken later when attacked by a chlorine radical in the propagation step.
options.B: Correct. Light causes homolytic fission of Cl2 into two Cl radicals. This is the initiation step that provides the reactive species needed for the chain reaction to continue.
options.C: Light causes homolysis to form neutral atoms (radicals), not heterolysis to form ions. Ions like Cl+ and Cl- would require a polar solvent and a different mechanism, electrophilic, not free radical.
options.D: Heating is not the function here. While heat can also initiate radicals, in this experiment light (uv) supplies the activation energy photochemically, not by simply warming the mixture.
